title: The ban is moral and perpetual—Gentiles are reproached for image-cult, not for breaching Moses’ positive rites
source_text: XVII. Et certe legem illam positivam non esse, quae solos Judaeos spectaret, sed moralem quae omnes homines in universum, & semper obstringit, inde manifestum est, quod imaginum cultus, & earum fabricatio, ad numen repraesentandum, in Dei verbo gentibus exprobratur, ut passim apud Prophetas videre est. Nec enim gentibus vitio verti solet, quod leges positivas, Israelitico populo a Mose datas, transgressae sint; sed solum quod legem moralem, per naturam hominum cordibus impressam violarint.
pass_a_gloss: And certainly that that law is not positive, which would regard the Jews alone, but moral, which binds all men universally, and always, is thence manifest, that the cult of images, and their fabrication, for representing the divinity, is reproached to the Gentiles in the word of God, as is to be seen everywhere among the Prophets. For it is not customarily turned to the fault of the Gentiles that they transgressed the positive laws given by Moses to the Israelite people; but only that they violated the moral law impressed by nature on the hearts of men.
pass_b_english: Prophets blame Gentiles for making and culting images—proof the ban is moral for all, not a Jew-only positive rite.
Gentiles are not charged with breaking Moses’ ceremonial code, but with violating nature’s moral law.

choices.why: Natural-law grounding of the moral ban.
